sections.title: Symmetric matrices with positive eigenvalues; $S = A^TA$
sections.summary: Oscillation $y'' + Sy = 0$ needs the eigenvalues $\lambda = \omega^2$ of the symmetric $S$ to be nonnegative. $S$ is positive definite when all its eigenvalues are positive, semidefinite when they are $\ge 0$. Every $A^TA$ is at least semidefinite, because $x^TA^TAx = \|Ax\|^2$.
goals: Define positive definite and positive semidefinite.
Show that the eigenvalues of $A^TA$ are $\ge 0$.

notes.heading: Why positive eigenvalues matter
paragraphs: In $y'' + Sy = 0$, try $y = e^{i\omega t}x$: $-\omega^2x + Sx = 0$, so $Sx = \omega^2x$. A real frequency $\omega$ needs $\lambda = \omega^2 \ge 0$. A negative eigenvalue would give $e^{\pm\sqrt{-\lambda}t}$, exponential growth instead of oscillation.
$S$ is positive definite if it is symmetric and every eigenvalue is positive; positive semidefinite if every eigenvalue is $\ge 0$ (zero allowed).

notes.heading: Every A transpose A
paragraphs: $S = A^TA$ is symmetric for any rectangular $A$. If $Sx = \lambda x$, multiply by $x^T$: $x^TA^TAx = \lambda x^Tx$. The left side is $(Ax)^T(Ax) = \|Ax\|^2 \ge 0$ and $x^Tx > 0$, so $\lambda \ge 0$. If the columns of $A$ are independent, $Ax \neq 0$ for $x \neq 0$ and every $\lambda > 0$: $A^TA$ is positive definite.

example.title: A transpose A (authored)
example.problem: For $A = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 2\\ 0 & 1\\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}$, find $S = A^TA$ and its eigenvalues.

steps.text: Dot products of the columns (1, 0, 1) and (2, 1, 0).
Both positive, as the independent columns guarantee.

book.label: Section 7.2: positive definite matrices and the SVD

sections.tutorNotes: Video 48, first part. y'' + Sy = 0, y = e^(i omega t) x: Sx = omega^2 x, need lambda >= 0. Positive definite: symmetric, all lambda > 0; semidefinite: lambda >= 0. S = A^T A: x^T A^T A x = ||Ax||^2 >= 0 so lambda >= 0; independent columns give lambda > 0.

sections.title: Five equivalent tests, and the energy bowl $x^TSx$
sections.summary: For symmetric $S$ these are equivalent: all eigenvalues $> 0$; all pivots $> 0$; all upper-left determinants $> 0$; $S = A^TA$ with independent columns; energy $x^TSx > 0$ for every $x \neq 0$. For $S = \begin{bmatrix}4&6\\6&10\end{bmatrix}$ the energy $4x_1^2 + 12x_1x_2 + 10x_2^2$ is a bowl with its minimum at the origin.
goals: Apply all five tests to a $2\times2$ matrix.
Write the energy $x^TSx$ as a quadratic.
Picture positive definite energy as a bowl.
Test a $3\times3$ correlation matrix with determinants.

notes.heading: Five tests
paragraphs: $S = \begin{bmatrix}4 & 6\\ 6 & 10\end{bmatrix}$. (1) Eigenvalues: trace $14$, determinant $4$, both roots positive. (2) Pivots: elimination subtracts $\tfrac32$ of row 1 from row 2, leaving pivots $4$ and $10 - 9 = 1$. (3) Upper-left determinants: $4$ and $40 - 36 = 4$. (4) $S = A^TA$ for an $A$ with independent columns, for instance from elimination ($S = LDL^T$ gives $A = \sqrt{D}L^T$). (5) Energy: $x^TSx > 0$ for $x \neq 0$.
The tests agree for every symmetric matrix; use whichever is easiest. In practice the pivots (elimination) are the fastest.

notes.heading: Energy
paragraphs: $x^TSx = 4x_1^2 + 12x_1x_2 + 10x_2^2$ (the off-diagonal $6$ appears twice). At $x = (1, 1)$: $4 + 12 + 10 = 26$; at $x = (1, -1)$: $4 - 12 + 10 = 2$. Completing the square, $4(x_1 + \tfrac32x_2)^2 + x_2^2$: the pivots $4$ and $1$ appear as the coefficients, and both squares are positive.

The graph of the energy is a bowl opening upward with its minimum at $x = 0$; its level curves are ellipses whose axes are the eigenvectors. This is the second-derivative test for a minimum in two variables.

notes.heading: A 3 by 3 test
paragraphs: A correlation matrix $\begin{bmatrix}1 & a & b\\ a & 1 & c\\ b & c & 1\end{bmatrix}$ is positive definite when its upper-left determinants are positive: $1 > 0$, $1 - a^2 > 0$, and $1 + 2abc - a^2 - b^2 - c^2 > 0$.

keyIdeas: Positive definite energy: a bowl, elliptic level curves.

example.title: A matrix that fails (authored)
example.problem: Is $S = \begin{bmatrix}3 & 4\\ 4 & 5\end{bmatrix}$ positive definite? Find an $x$ with negative energy.
example.answer: No: the determinant and the second pivot are negative, and $x = (4, -3)$ has energy $-3$. The energy surface is a saddle, not a bowl.

sections.tutorNotes: Video 48. Five equivalent tests for symmetric S: eigenvalues > 0, pivots > 0, upper-left determinants > 0, S = A^T A with independent columns, energy x^T S x > 0 for x != 0. S = [4 6; 6 10]: trace 14, det 4, pivots 4 and 1, determinants 4 and 4; energy 4x1^2 + 12x1x2 + 10x2^2 = 4(x1 + 1.5 x2)^2 + x2^2; x = (1,1) gives 26, (1,-1) gives 2. Bowl, elliptic level curves. Correlation matrix [1 a b; a 1 c; b c 1]: 1 - a^2 > 0, 1 + 2abc - a^2 - b^2 - c^2 > 0.

sections.title: The singular value decomposition $A = U\Sigma V^T$
sections.summary: Every matrix, even rectangular, factors as $A = U\Sigma V^T$: rotate or reflect ($V^T$), stretch ($\Sigma$, the singular values $\sigma_i \ge 0$), rotate ($U$). The $v$'s are eigenvectors of $A^TA$, the $u$'s eigenvectors of $AA^T$, and $\sigma_i^2$ are their eigenvalues. $A = \sigma_1u_1v_1^T + \sigma_2u_2v_2^T + \cdots$, and the first piece carries the most information.
goals: Describe $A = U\Sigma V^T$ as rotate (or reflect), stretch, rotate (or reflect).
Compute the SVD of a singular $2\times2$ matrix.
Write $A$ as a sum of rank-one pieces and explain their use for data.

notes.heading: Rotate, stretch, rotate (or reflect)
paragraphs: Eigenvectors need a square matrix and may fail to be orthogonal. The SVD works for every $m\times n$ matrix with orthogonal matrices on both sides: $A = U\Sigma V^T$ with $U$ ($m\times m$) and $V$ ($n\times n$) orthogonal and $\Sigma$ ($m\times n$) diagonal with $\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \cdots \ge 0$. Geometrically, $A$ turns the unit circle into an ellipse: $V^T$ turns the plane, $\Sigma$ stretches along the axes, $U$ turns it again. Each orthogonal factor is a rotation or a reflection: for $A = \mathrm{diag}(1, -1)$, which flips the plane, no pair of rotations can do it, and $U$ (or $V$) must be a reflection.

notes.heading: Where U, Sigma and V come from
paragraphs: $A^TA = V\Sigma^TU^TU\Sigma V^T = V(\Sigma^T\Sigma)V^T$: this is the diagonalization of the symmetric semidefinite $A^TA$. So the $v$'s are its orthonormal eigenvectors and $\sigma_i^2$ its eigenvalues. Likewise $AA^T = U(\Sigma\Sigma^T)U^T$ gives the $u$'s. In practice, find $v_i$ and $\sigma_i$ from $A^TA$ and then $u_i = Av_i/\sigma_i$ for $\sigma_i > 0$.

notes.heading: The lecture's example
paragraphs: $A = \begin{bmatrix}2 & 2\\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}$ is singular (rank $1$). $A^TA = \begin{bmatrix}5 & 5\\ 5 & 5\end{bmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $10$ and $0$, so $\sigma_1 = \sqrt{10}$, $\sigma_2 = 0$, with $v_1 = (1, 1)/\sqrt2$, $v_2 = (1, -1)/\sqrt2$. Then $u_1 = Av_1/\sigma_1 = (2, 1)/\sqrt5$, and $u_2 = (-1, 2)/\sqrt5$ completes an orthonormal basis.
Note: on the board the matrix is first written with a $-1$ and then corrected to make it singular; the lower-left entry of $U$ keeps the old sign there. For the singular $A$, $u_1 = (2, 1)/\sqrt5$.

notes.heading: Rank-one pieces and data
paragraphs: Multiplying out, $A = \sigma_1u_1v_1^T + \sigma_2u_2v_2^T + \cdots$, a sum of rank-one matrices ordered by importance. For a data matrix (say, gene expressions: genes $\times$ people), the first piece $\sigma_1u_1v_1^T$ captures the strongest pattern linking a combination of genes to a combination of people. Keeping only the largest few pieces is principal component analysis.

keyIdeas: $A = U\Sigma V^T$: rotate or reflect, stretch, rotate or reflect.

steps.text: Left singular vectors u = Av / sigma.

A^T A = V Sigma^T Sigma V^T
Sigma squared are eigenvalues of A^T A

sections.tutorNotes: Video 49. A = U Sigma V^T for any m x n A: U, V orthogonal, Sigma diagonal sigma1 >= sigma2 >= ... >= 0; rotate/reflect-stretch-rotate. A^T A = V Sigma^T Sigma V^T (v's, sigma^2), A A^T = U Sigma Sigma^T U^T (u's); u_i = A v_i / sigma_i. Example A = [2 2; 1 1] (singular; board first had a -1): sigma = sqrt10, 0; v1 = (1,1)/sqrt2, v2 = (1,-1)/sqrt2; u1 = (2,1)/sqrt5, u2 = (-1,2)/sqrt5. A = sum sigma_i u_i v_i^T; first piece most important (gene expression data, PCA).

quiz.question: Why does $y'' + Sy = 0$ oscillate only when the eigenvalues of $S$ are $\ge 0$?

choices.why: No. $y''$ changes sign as $y$ oscillates.
Right. A negative eigenvalue gives exponential growth $e^{\sqrt{-\lambda}t}$.
No. Any symmetric $S$ works.
No. Only the signs of the eigenvalues matter.

quiz.question: Why are the eigenvalues of $A^TA$ never negative?

choices.why: No. $A^TA$ is symmetric, not usually diagonal.
No. Entries of any sign give the same conclusion.
No. Its determinant is $(\det A)^2$ for square $A$, which can be anything $\ge 0$.

choices.text: $x^TA^TAx = \|Ax\|^2 \ge 0$, and this equals $\lambda\|x\|^2$ for an eigenvector.
choices.why: Right. A squared length cannot be negative.
Right. $10 - \tfrac{6}{4}\cdot6 = 1$.
No. Elimination changes the second diagonal entry.
No. $4$ and $4$ are the upper-left determinants.
No. Those are close to the eigenvalues ($7 \pm 3\sqrt5$), not pivots.

quiz.question: For $S = \begin{bmatrix}4 & 6\\ 6 & 10\end{bmatrix}$, what is the energy at $x = (1, -1)$?

choices.why: No. Positive definite energy is never negative.
No. The cross term $12x_1x_2$ is $-12$ here.
No. That is at $x = (1, 1)$.

quiz.question: Which symmetric matrix is NOT positive definite?

choices.why: No. Pivots $4$ and $1$.
No. A diagonal matrix with positive entries.
Right. Its determinant is $15 - 16 = -1$.
No. Determinants $2$ and $3$, eigenvalues $1$ and $3$.

quiz.question: What does the graph of a positive definite energy $x^TSx$ look like?

choices.text: A bowl with its maximum at the origin
choices.why: No. That would be negative definite.

choices.text: A bowl with its minimum at the origin, elliptic level curves
choices.why: Right. Positive in every direction away from $0$.
No. A saddle has negative energy in some direction (indefinite $S$).
No. The energy is quadratic, not linear.
No. Only $\Sigma$ stretches.

choices.text: It exists only for square symmetric matrices.
choices.why: No. Every matrix, even rectangular, has an SVD.
No. $U = V$ only when $A$ is symmetric positive semidefinite.

choices.text: Rotate or reflect by $V^T$, stretch by $\Sigma$, rotate or reflect by $U$
choices.why: Right. Orthogonal, diagonal, orthogonal; an orthogonal factor can be a reflection, as for $A = \mathrm{diag}(1, -1)$.

quiz.question: Where do the singular values come from?

choices.why: Right. $A^TA = V\Sigma^T\Sigma V^T$.
No. For nonsymmetric $A$ they differ; $[2\ 2;\ 1\ 1]$ has eigenvalues $3, 0$ but $\sigma = \sqrt{10}, 0$.
No. They come from $A^TA$.
No. Pivots are a different factorization.

quiz.question: What are the singular values of $\begin{bmatrix}2 & 2\\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}$?

choices.why: No. Those are entries of $A$.
Right. $A^TA = \begin{bmatrix}5&5\\5&5\end{bmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $10$ and $0$.
No. $3$ and $0$ are the eigenvalues of $A$.
No. Take square roots of the eigenvalues of $A^TA$.

quiz.question: In $A = \sigma_1u_1v_1^T + \sigma_2u_2v_2^T + \cdots$, which piece matters most for a data matrix?

choices.why: No. Their sizes are the singular values.

choices.text: The piece with the largest entry of $u$
choices.why: No. Every $u_i$ is a unit vector; $\sigma_i$ measures the size.
Right. It captures the strongest pattern; keeping the top pieces is principal component analysis.
No. It has the smallest $\sigma$.
